939.title: Vivekananda (Chicago 1893
939.hook: a young monk stands up in Chicago and his first five words are a greeting
939.howItsDone: Vivekananda's Chicago addresses are printed in his Complete Works, and Hindu and Vedanta groups read them aloud in study circles and at gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna's lizard on the tree: every color, and sometimes no color at all. Today, one of the young men who sat in his room.

Chicago. A big hall, a platform crowded with delegates from many religions, each waiting a turn to speak. Among them is a young Hindu monk. In Ramakrishna's room he was called Narendranath. Here he's Swami Vivekananda, a long way from Bengal. When his turn finally comes, he stands up, faces the crowd, and opens not with an argument or a defense of his tradition, but with a greeting.
screen: `CHICAGO.` → `A YOUNG MONK FROM BENGAL.` → `HE OPENS WITH A GREETING.`

segments.voice: The occasion was the World's Parliament of Religions, and his short talk on the opening day is printed in his collected works as the response to the welcome. His first words were: Sisters and Brothers of America. Tradition says the hall broke into applause before he could go on. Whatever the crowd heard in it, the greeting makes strangers into family before a single idea is offered. Then come the ideas. He thanks his listeners in the name of the monks of his order and of the Hindu people. His tradition, he says, taught him not only to tolerate other paths but to accept them. He gives two texts to show what he means. First, a hymn he says he learned as a boy: as rivers rising in different places all mingle their water in the sea, so the different paths people take, crooked or straight, all lead to you, Lord. Second, the Bhagavad Gita, where Krishna says, in effect: whoever comes to me, by whatever road, I reach them. Then he names what he hopes is ending: sectarianism, bigotry and fanaticism, which, he says, have filled the earth with violence. He hopes the bell that rang that morning to open the Parliament will turn out to be their death knell. A greeting, two old texts, one hope. He didn't arrive with a new teaching. He carried in songs and verses from home.
screen: `SISTERS AND BROTHERS OF AMERICA.` · `NOT ONLY TOLERATE, BUT ACCEPT.` · `RIVERS INTO ONE SEA.` · `A BELL FOR THE END OF FANATICISM.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a room you'll walk into soon, an office, a classroom, a family dinner, and picture the people in it, especially the ones who are hard for you. Silently greet them the way he greeted Chicago, as sisters and brothers, without forcing a feeling, and notice what happens when you reach the difficult faces. If you pray, you can hold that room in a prayer you already know.
Vivekananda. Ramakrishna's disciple, the monk who greeted a hall in Chicago as sisters and brothers before saying anything else.
Your line: sisters and brothers of America. A greeting can do its work before any argument starts. See you tomorrow.

940.title: Vivekananda (Chicago 1893
940.hook: an Upanishad line read out in Chicago: hear, children of immortal bliss
940.howItsDone: Vivekananda's paper on Hinduism is read in Vedanta study circles, and the Upanishad's call to the children of immortal bliss is chanted and quoted in Hindu talks and gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vivekananda greeted a hall in Chicago as sisters and brothers, with a hymn of many rivers meeting in one sea.

Hear, children of immortal bliss. That's an old line from the Upanishads, and some days after his greeting, Vivekananda read it out to the same hall in Chicago. Not ladies and gentlemen. Not friends. Not even sisters and brothers this time. Children of immortal bliss: every person in the room, named for what he believed they already were. Today, his longer talk, the one printed as his paper on Hinduism.
screen: `HEAR, CHILDREN OF IMMORTAL BLISS.` → `READ OUT IN CHICAGO.` → `WHAT YOU ALREADY ARE.`

segments.voice: The line comes from the Shvetashvatara Upanishad, where a seer calls out to all the children of the immortal and says, in effect: I have known the great one, shining like the sun, beyond the darkness, and only by knowing that does anyone pass beyond death. Vivekananda turns that call toward his listeners. They are not, at bottom, weak or fallen creatures, he tells them. He calls them children of God, sharers of immortal bliss, and holy. The soul, in the Vedanta he describes, was never born and never dies; body and mind change, but what you are underneath does not. Then a second move. Religion, he says, is not finally about accepting a doctrine or agreeing with a creed. It's about realizing: being, and becoming. In the Hindu view he lays out, the point is to see the divine directly, not just to hear about it. Images, rituals and scriptures are helps along the road, steps for different people at different places. For the Hindu, he says, a person isn't traveling from error to truth, but from truth to truth, from a lower truth to a higher one. A lower step isn't an error; it's simply where someone stands. So the paper holds two things together: a very high claim about every person in the room, and a very patient view of how people get there. Children of immortal bliss, still learning to walk.
screen: `A SEER CALLS OUT TO EVERYONE.` · `NOT WEAK, BUT HOLY.` · `RELIGION IS REALIZING.` · `FROM TRUTH TO TRUTH.`

If you pray, you can rest in a prayer you already know.
Vivekananda. The monk who stood in Chicago and called his listeners children of immortal bliss.

941.title: Vivekananda (Chicago 1893
941.hook: a frog who has never left his well meets a frog from the sea
941.carry: nothing can be bigger than my well
941.howItsDone: Vivekananda's frog in the well is retold in Hindu talks, interfaith gatherings and school lessons as a picture of a narrow view, with the speaker himself counted among the frogs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Upanishad's call that Vivekananda read out in Chicago: hear, children of immortal bliss.

A frog lives at the bottom of a well. He was born there, and he's done well for himself: he's fat, he's healthy, and he keeps the water clean of worms and bugs. One day another frog falls in. This one comes from the sea. The well frog is curious, and a little suspicious. Where are you from? The sea. And how big is the sea? Vivekananda told this story in Chicago, a few days into the Parliament, after speakers had been disagreeing.
screen: `A FROG IN A WELL.` → `A FROG FROM THE SEA FALLS IN.` → `HOW BIG IS THE SEA?`

segments.voice: In his short talk called Why We Disagree, he lets the story play out. Is the sea as big as my well? the frog asks, and he leaps from one side of the well to the other. Bigger, says the sea frog. A bigger leap. This big? Much bigger. You can't compare the sea with your well. So the well frog decides the visitor must be lying. Nothing can be bigger than my well, he says. Throw him out. Here's the turn. Vivekananda doesn't point the story at any one group in the hall. He puts himself in it first: he's a Hindu, he says, sitting in his own little well and thinking the whole world is that well. Then he names the others the same way. Each of us is sitting in a little well and taking it for the world. He even thanks his American hosts for trying to break down the walls of those little worlds. That's the gentleness in it. The joke isn't on the frog for living in a well. Everyone has to live somewhere, and this frog keeps his water clean. The trouble starts only at one sentence: nothing can be bigger than my well. He tells it like a joke, but it carries the same hope as his greeting: not that anyone leaves home, but that people stop throwing out every visitor who says the water goes farther than they've seen.
screen: `THE FROG LEAPS ACROSS HIS WELL.` · `THROW HIM OUT, HE'S LYING.` · `"I'M SITTING IN MY OWN WELL."` · `EVERYONE HAS A WELL.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind your own well: the neighborhood, the family, the group or the way of seeing you grew up inside, and notice what's good about it, the water you keep clean. Then remember one time someone told you the world was bigger than that, and you didn't want to hear it. No judging; just breathe there, and notice the frog's leap, measuring the sea against the walls.
Vivekananda. The monk who told the Chicago Parliament he was a frog in his own well, too.
Your line: nothing can be bigger than my well. Tomorrow, his book on the yoga of work. Day nine hundred forty-one, done.

942.title: Karma Yoga
942.hook: a chapter title that sounds backwards: we help ourselves, not the world
942.carry: the giver is the one who says thank you
942.howItsDone: Hindu service groups, including those of the Ramakrishna order, describe their work as seva, service offered as worship, and Vivekananda's Karma Yoga is read in Vedanta study circles alongside the Bhagavad Gita.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the frog in the well, and a monk who said he was sitting in his own well too. Your line: nothing can be bigger than my well.

Saturday morning, a folding table outside a shelter, and a volunteer handing out sandwiches. She's tired, a little proud of herself, and every so often she waits for a thank-you that doesn't come. Vivekananda, back from Chicago and lecturing in America, gave a whole talk about it. Its title sounds backwards: we help ourselves, not the world.
screen: `A VOLUNTEER WAITS FOR THANKS.` → `A TITLE THAT SOUNDS BACKWARDS.` → `WE HELP OURSELVES, NOT THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: Karma Yoga is a set of Vivekananda's talks on work, gathered as a book. In the chapter called We Help Ourselves, Not the World, he starts by taking some air out of the helper. The world isn't waiting for any one of us to rescue it, he says. It will go on, with or without our help. That sounds harsh until you see where he's going. If the world doesn't need us, then helping is not a favor we do it. It's a chance we're given. He calls the world a great moral gymnasium, where we all exercise so that we grow stronger. The person you help is the one who lets you into the gym. So he turns the usual thank-you around. Don't stand over someone and say, here, poor fellow, take this. Stand thankful that they let you give. The blessing, he says, is to the giver. Then one step further, straight from his Vedanta: serve the person in front of you as you would worship God, because, in the Vedanta he teaches, the divine is present in them. Not pity from above. Worship, from slightly below. Back at the table, the wait for thanks has nothing to hang on. She isn't owed anything; she's the one who got the workout. And the person taking the sandwich isn't a project. In his picture, they're the one doing her a kindness.
screen: `THE WORLD DOESN'T NEED RESCUING.` · `A GREAT MORAL GYMNASIUM.` · `THE GIVER SAYS THANK YOU.` · `SERVE AS WORSHIP.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've helped lately, a coworker, a parent, a stranger, a child, and notice if any part of you is still waiting for their thanks or keeping a small score. No need to scold that part; just turn it around, the way the chapter does, and silently thank them for letting you help, seeing their face as you do. If you pray, you can hold them in a prayer you already know.

943.title: Karma Yoga
943.hook: a fly lands on a pot of honey to sip, and finds its feet stuck
943.carry: keep your feet on the rim
943.howItsDone: Hindus who follow the Bhagavad Gita's teaching on work describe offering their work to God without clinging to its results, and Vedanta study circles read Vivekananda's Karma Yoga alongside the Gita.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karma Yoga's moral gymnasium, where the giver is the one who says thank you.

A fly finds a pot of honey. What luck. It lands on the rim, walks down to the sweet part, and starts to drink. A minute later it tries to lift off, and can't. Its feet are stuck in the very thing it came to enjoy. Vivekananda uses a picture like this in his talks on Karma Yoga, and it isn't really about flies. It's about a new job, a relationship, a project, a phone.
screen: `A FLY FINDS HONEY.` → `IT COMES TO SIP.` → `ITS FEET ARE STUCK.`

segments.voice: His diagnosis comes in a run of short reversals. We came to enjoy, and we're being enjoyed. We came to rule, and we're being ruled. We came to work, and we're being worked. The honey isn't the problem. Work isn't the problem either; again and again he tells people to work. The trouble is the sticking: work done for what it will get us, so that the getting owns us. So how do you drink without getting stuck? Not by staying away from the honey. Running from the world doesn't free anyone. The answer he calls non-attachment, and he offers two roads to it, for two kinds of people. If you believe in God, there's the road of the Bhagavad Gita: work, and give the results away to God, the way you'd lay a flower at a shrine. The work is yours to do. What comes of it isn't yours to clutch. And if you don't believe in God, he doesn't send you away. He offers the road of reflection and will: keep telling yourself, this outcome is not me, this praise is not me, this failure is not me, until it's true. Listeners who pray and listeners who don't, and he hands each of them something to use on Monday. The fly can still drink. It just learns to keep its feet on the rim.
screen: `WE CAME TO WORK; WE'RE BEING WORKED.` · `DON'T RUN FROM THE HONEY.` · `ROAD ONE: GIVE THE RESULTS TO GOD.` · `ROAD TWO: THIS IS NOT ME.`

segments.voice: Name one thing you're working on that you care about a lot, and notice where your feet are stuck: a result you need, someone's approval, a number. If you pray, picture setting that result down at a shrine and leaving it there; if you don't, say silently on each out-breath, this result is not me. Either way, keep caring about the work, and just lift one foot off the honey.
Karma Yoga. The yoga of work: drinking the honey without getting stuck in it.
Your line: keep your feet on the rim. Tomorrow, two scenes from one afternoon. Day nine hundred forty-three.

944.title: Karma Yoga
944.hook: a warm speech at a party, and twenty minutes later, the same man in the parking lot
944.carry: character lives in the common actions
944.howItsDone: Hindus who read Vivekananda's Karma Yoga in Vedanta study circles discuss its first chapter on character, and some describe the practice as bringing care to everyday work, not only to special occasions.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the fly in the honey, and Karma Yoga's answer: drink, but keep your feet on the rim.
screen: `KARMA YOGA.` · `KEEP YOUR FEET ON THE RIM.`

segments.voice: Two scenes from one afternoon. In the first, a man gives the toast at a retirement party. He's funny, he's generous, he names everyone who helped. People wipe their eyes. In the second, twenty minutes later, he's in the parking lot, leaning on his horn at an old man who is backing out too slowly. Which scene is the real him? Early in his talks on Karma Yoga, Vivekananda asks where a person's real character shows, and his answer points away from the toast.
screen: `A WARM TOAST AT A PARTY.` → `THE SAME MAN IN THE PARKING LOT.` → `WHICH ONE IS HIM?`

segments.voice: The first chapter of Karma Yoga is about what work does to character. Early on, Vivekananda says something that sounds simple and isn't. Don't judge a person by their great moments. Big occasions, he says, can lift almost anyone up for a while; even an ordinary person can be a hero once. Watch them instead doing the most common things. That's where the real character shows. Then he explains why. Every action we take, and every thought we think, leaves a mark on the mind, like a wave on a lake that sinks back down but leaves the water changed. Hindu thought calls these marks samskaras, impressions. A person's character, he says, is really the sum of these impressions, piled up over time. Good impressions, repeated, make a tendency toward good. Careless ones, repeated, make a tendency too. So the parking lot isn't a slip from the real man. It's a window into the pile. And here's what makes this a yoga and not just a warning. If small actions build character, then small actions are where the work gets done. Not the toast, which happens once. The horn, the email tone, the way you hand someone their change, which happen every day. Each one lays down the next layer of who you'll be tomorrow.
screen: `DON'T JUDGE BY THE GREAT MOMENTS.` · `WATCH THE MOST COMMON THINGS.` · `EVERY ACT LEAVES AN IMPRESSION.` · `CHARACTER IS THE PILE OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Replay one ordinary moment from yesterday, a meal, a commute, a line at a counter: how did you speak, what did your hands do, was there a flash of impatience or a small kindness? Don't judge it; just notice what impression it may have left. Then picture one ordinary moment coming up today done with care, and if you pray, offer it in a prayer you already know.
Karma Yoga. The yoga of work, and of the common actions where Vivekananda says character is really built.
Your line: character lives in the common actions. Tomorrow, a desert in the middle of a city. See you then.

945.title: Karma Yoga
945.hook: a quiet desert inside a rush-hour street, and the week's last look at the yoga of work
945.carry: a desert in the busy street
945.howItsDone: Hindus who follow Vivekananda's teaching on Karma Yoga describe aiming to stay inwardly calm while working fully, and his talks are read in Vedanta study circles alongside the Bhagavad Gita.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the toast and the parking lot: character lives in the common actions, each one leaving an impression.

Where would you go to find silence? A cave, a retreat, an empty chapel on a weekday, a desert. In his talks on Karma Yoga, Vivekananda moves the desert. He sets it down in the streets of a big city, in all their traffic. Picture it today as a train station at rush hour, announcements overhead, someone running for a door that's already closing. Busy hands, and somewhere inside, a desert. He calls the person who can hold both an ideal.
screen: `WHERE DO YOU GO FOR SILENCE?` → `HE MOVES THE DESERT.` → `INTO THE STATION AT RUSH HOUR.`

segments.voice: Here's the ideal, in his own picture. The ideal person, Vivekananda says, is one who, in the deepest silence and solitude, finds intense activity, and in the middle of intense activity finds the silence and solitude of the desert. It runs both ways. Silence with life inside it. Busyness with a desert inside it. This person, he adds, has learned self-control and can't be shaken by what's happening around them. Now look back at the week. It began in Chicago, with a young monk greeting a hall of strangers as sisters and brothers, and reading an Upanishad line that called everyone children of immortal bliss. Then a frog in a well, and the reminder that every well is small. Then the books of work: the world as a moral gymnasium, where the giver says thank you; the fly in the honey, learning to drink without getting stuck; and the parking lot, where character is built out of common actions. Every one is about the same skill: staying in the middle of the action without being swept off by it. That's the desert inside the station. Not escaping the noise. Being quiet enough within it to work well. Which raises a question: how do you actually find that quiet? Karma Yoga mostly answers with work itself. But Vivekananda has another book that goes straight at the mind, and that's tomorrow.
screen: `SILENCE WITH ACTIVITY INSIDE IT.` · `ACTIVITY WITH A DESERT INSIDE IT.` · `THE WEEK: CHICAGO, GYMNASIUM, HONEY, HABITS.` · `HOW DO YOU FIND THE QUIET?`

segments.voice: For the first part of the sit, let the world in: every sound, every itch, every thought about what's next, without pushing any of it away. Then, changing nothing outside, look for the still place underneath, the part of you noticing the noise that isn't noisy itself, and rest there while the sounds go on. If you pray, you can hold that stillness in a prayer you already know.
Karma Yoga. The yoga of work, whose ideal is a calm desert in the middle of the busiest street.
